title: A Pre-Sale Is a Promise Sold Before the Product Exists
summary: Selling homes before they are built does three jobs at once: it proves demand to a lender, it discovers the price and it transfers part of the market risk to buyers. It also creates a duty of honesty and safekeeping that lasts until the buyer gets the keys. This lesson sets out how to think about pre-sales, pricing against absorption and the channels you sell through.
body:
A pre-sale is not a sale of a home. It is a sale of a promise to deliver a home, and everything about pre-selling well follows from treating that promise, and the buyer's deposit behind it, as something you hold in trust until you deliver.

Recall

Q. What is a time bar in a construction contract?

A. A clause making timely written notice a condition precedent to a claim, so that notice given late can defeat the claim whatever its merits.

Q. In Week 122, what was the owner's meeting cadence for?

A. To make sure every decision and escalation happens at a known time, with the right people and the right records, so that problems surface early rather than on the day they become urgent.

Q. What is a hold point in an inspection and test plan?

A. A step at which work must stop until a named inspector has inspected and signed it off.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the first week of Phase 13, Selling, Owning and Growing. Up to now you have learned to finance, design and build. Now you learn to turn a building into revenue. For a for-sale project, that starts long before construction, because many construction lenders will not fund until a defined share of the units is sold. The pre-sale campaign is therefore not a marketing activity bolted onto the end. It is a condition of the loan, a test of your price and a legal relationship with every buyer that runs for two or three years.

This lesson teaches concepts. It does not script how to approach any real buyer or investor, and it does not state what the law requires where you sell. LEX covers the rules on Day 4.

What a pre-sale actually does

In plain English: you sign a buyer to a contract to buy a unit when it is finished, take a deposit, and use the stack of signed contracts to prove the project is real.

The professional framing gives a pre-sale three jobs. First, demand proof. A lender's pre-sale threshold is a condition requiring a minimum level of firm sales before first draw, often expressed as a share of units or as sale proceeds covering a share of the loan. The level is commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal, not a standard. Second, price discovery. The first buyers tell you, with money rather than opinion, what the market will pay. Third, risk transfer. A buyer who has signed and paid a deposit carries part of the market risk, because if prices fall the deposit is at stake.

That third job is also the danger. A buyer who loses money on a falling market may walk away and forfeit the deposit, or may refuse to close and test whether the contract binds. Pre-sales only transfer risk if the deposits are meaningful, the contracts are enforceable and the buyers are real.

Pricing against absorption

In plain English: the price you set decides how fast you sell, and how fast you sell decides your carrying cost and your loan.

Absorption is the number of units the market takes up per month at a given price. From Week 28, you know absorption is a number, not a feeling. In pre-sales it becomes a lever. Price too high and the campaign stalls below the lender's threshold, so construction cannot start and pre-construction costs keep running. Price too low and you hit the threshold fast but leave value on the table for the whole building.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 100-unit project. At an average of 500,000 dollars a unit, your market study says the market will absorb about 4 units a month. At 475,000 dollars, a 5 percent reduction, it absorbs about 7 a month. The lender needs 60 units sold. At the higher price that is 15 months of selling; at the lower price, about 9 months. If pre-construction carrying costs, such as land interest, design fees and marketing, run 150,000 dollars a month, the faster campaign saves 6 months, or 900,000 dollars of carry, and starts the building 6 months earlier. Against that, a 25,000-dollar discount on 60 units costs 1,500,000 dollars. On these numbers the higher price is worth more, unless the slower campaign also risks a market turn before you hit the threshold. That risk is the real decision, and it is a judgement about the cycle, not arithmetic.

Say that out loud now.

Releasing, not dumping

Experienced developers rarely release every unit at once. They release in phases or tranches: a first group at an opening price to build momentum and test demand, then later groups at higher prices as the building becomes more real. This is a price ladder. It rewards early buyers for taking more risk and lets you raise prices on evidence. The control is honesty: every price, incentive and condition offered must be recorded, so that the same unit is never sold on different terms to two people and the lender sees the true average.

Channels, including buyers abroad

A channel is the route by which buyers reach you: your own sales office, external brokers, a marketing agency, a referral network, or buyers living abroad, including a diaspora who want a home in the place they came from. Each channel has a cost, usually a commission or fee, and a risk profile. Brokers paid only on signing may push buyers who will not close. Buyers abroad bring their own questions: they earn in another currency, may need overseas mortgages, are harder to verify for identity and source of funds, and may face rules on foreign ownership or extra taxes in some places. Treat each channel as a pipeline with a cost per firm sale and a closing rate, not as a volume figure.

A second worked example. Channel A, your own office, signs 20 buyers at a cost of 5,000 dollars each and 95 percent close. Channel B, an overseas agent, signs 20 buyers at 15,000 dollars each and 80 percent close. Cost per closed sale is about 5,260 dollars for A and 18,750 dollars for B. Channel B may still be worth it if it reaches buyers A cannot, but you now know its real price.

How the best do it

The strongest residential developers treat a pre-sale campaign as an underwritten process. They test demand with a soft registration list before setting prices, release in tranches, report sales to the lender monthly with each buyer's deposit status, and audit their brokers' files for identity checks. A small developer can copy the whole discipline cheaply: one sales ledger, one deposit trust or escrow arrangement, one monthly report and no unrecorded side deals.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: deposits, sale timing and how gains are recognised can change tax outcomes; ask a tax adviser before the sales contract is fixed. Liability: marketing statements can become misrepresentation claims, so every claim must be true and provable. Banking: the pre-sale threshold is a loan condition, and the lender will audit the contracts. Governance: one person approves prices, incentives and contract changes. Estate: an heir inherits obligations to every buyer, so the sales file must be complete. Exit: closings are the exit, and their pace sets your return.

Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer admitted where you sell, for the purchase contract, disclosure and deposit handling.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is selling contracts that will not close: buyers who cannot finance, cannot be verified or were sold on promises you cannot keep. The control is a qualified sales ledger: identity and source-of-funds checks, meaningful deposits, written terms only and closing-rate tracking by channel.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts signatures. The lender, and the market, count closings. Report both.

Callback

In Week 41, Priya and LEX taught deposit structures, trust and escrow, and buyer default. This week puts those mechanics inside a campaign. The deposit rules are not paperwork after the sale; they decide whether the sale transfers any risk at all.

Recap

A pre-sale proves demand, discovers price and transfers some market risk, but only if deposits are meaningful, contracts bind and buyers are real. Price against absorption, release in tranches, price every channel by cost per closed sale and hold every deposit as if it belonged to the buyer, because until closing it largely does.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: Evergrande, and what happens when pre-sales fund everything.
checklist: I know the lender's pre-sale threshold and how it is measured, in units or in proceeds.
My price decision compares the cost of slower absorption with the cost of a lower price.
Units are released in recorded tranches, and every price and incentive is in the sales ledger.
Every channel is measured by cost per closed sale and closing rate, not signatures.
Every buyer has an identity and source-of-funds check before the contract is accepted.
Deposits go only into the trust or escrow arrangement my lawyer has confirmed.
No marketing claim is made that I cannot prove in writing.
I report signed, deposit-paid and expected-to-close numbers to the lender every month.
head: Field checklist
speak: A pre-sale is a sale of a promise to deliver a home, and the buyer's deposit is held for them until I deliver. Pre-sales do three jobs: they prove demand to a lender, which often sets a pre-sale threshold before first draw; they discover the price with real money; and they transfer some market risk to buyers. Price is a lever on absorption. In my hypothetical, cutting 5 percent sped the campaign from 15 months to about 9, saving 900,000 dollars of carry, but cost 1.5 million in discounts, so the decision turned on whether the slower campaign risked a market turn. I release in tranches on a price ladder and record every term. I measure each channel, including buyers abroad, by cost per closed sale. And I count closings, not signatures, because contracts that will not close transfer no risk at all.
terms: Pre-sale threshold — a lender's condition requiring a minimum level of firm unit sales, by count or proceeds, before construction funding begins.
Absorption — the number of units the market takes up per month at a given price and product.
Price ladder — releasing units in tranches at stepped prices, so early buyers are rewarded for risk and later prices rise on evidence of demand.

hostile.q: As your lender, how do I know your 60 pre-sales are real?
hostile.a: I will give you the full sales ledger: each contract, the buyer's verified identity, the deposit paid and confirmed by the trust or escrow holder, the channel and any incentive offered. You may audit any file. I also report which buyers have provided financing evidence, and I track closing rates by channel, so you see the sales I expect to close, not just the signatures.

title: Evergrande: When Pre-Sales Funded Everything
summary: China Evergrande grew by selling homes before they were built and using the cash to buy more land and start more projects. When credit tightened from 2020, the model stopped working, and buyers who had paid for unfinished homes were left waiting. Taken through the seven forensic steps, with Roman assisting on the finance, the case shows why a buyer's deposit must stay with the building it was paid for.
body:
Evergrande did not fail because it could not sell homes. It failed because the money from homes it had sold but not built was used to buy land and start new projects, so the whole company depended on selling faster next year than this year, and the day that stopped, the unfinished homes had no money behind them.

Recall

Q. What three jobs does a pre-sale do?

A. It proves demand to a lender, discovers the price with real money and transfers part of the market risk to the buyer, but only if deposits are meaningful, contracts bind and buyers are real.

Q. What is Rule 123?

A. Never let schedule pressure release a hold. Stripping and loading follow verified strength and the engineer's sequence, a low result stops loading until resolved, and no payment certifies work the monitor has not verified.

Q. What is a maturity wall?

A. A cluster of debt falling due in a short period, which becomes dangerous if the borrower cannot refinance all of it at once in a tight market.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Ford, with Roman assisting on the finance. Evergrande is one of the largest property failures on record, and it is useful to a small developer precisely because the mechanism is simple. Nothing in it requires a sophisticated product. It requires only that cash collected for one purpose is spent on another, and that growth hides the gap. I will keep to the public outline of events. Where accounts of the details differ, I leave the details out, and I quote no company figures.

1. Timeline

China Evergrande Group, a developer based in southern China, grew over the 2000s and 2010s into one of the country's largest home builders, with projects in a very large number of cities and businesses well beyond housing. In August 2020, Chinese regulators introduced leverage limits for property developers that became known as the three red lines, restricting new borrowing by companies that breached them. During 2021 the company struggled to pay suppliers, contractors and holders of investment products it had sold, and protests were reported at its offices. In December 2021, a rating agency declared it in default after missed payments on offshore bonds. Through 2022, buyers in a number of cities, across many developers' projects, publicly refused to keep paying mortgages on homes whose construction had stopped. In 2023 the company sought recognition of a restructuring in a United States court, and in January 2024 a court in Hong Kong ordered it to be wound up.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions carried the failure. Funding land acquisition and new starts with cash from pre-sales of homes not yet built. Expanding into businesses unrelated to the core, which consumed cash without adding to the ability to finish homes. And funding gaps with short-term debt and investment products sold to employees, suppliers and the public, which turned operating creditors into lenders who could not wait.

3. Assumptions

The model assumed that prices would keep rising, that sales would keep growing and that credit would keep rolling. Each assumption was reasonable in any single year of the boom. Together they meant the company needed every year to be better than the last. It also assumed, as many developers in many countries have, that a buyer who has paid a deposit is a source of funding. A deposit is a source of liquidity, but it carries an obligation to deliver, which is a liability, not equity.

Say that out loud now.

4. Incentives

The incentives all pointed at growth. Sales volume and land bank size were the measures the market rewarded. Local economies in many places relied heavily on land sales, and buyers were keen to buy early before prices rose. Contractors and suppliers kept working on promises of later payment because the company was large. Nobody in the chain was rewarded for asking whether the cash collected for each building was still available to finish that building.

5. Warning signs ignored

The signs were the classic ones. Very high leverage relative to equity. Heavy reliance on pre-sale cash and short-term borrowing. Payments to contractors stretched, and suppliers paid partly in instruments rather than cash. Sales of investment products to people with a relationship to the company. A regulatory signal, in the form of the leverage limits, that the credit environment had changed. Any one of these in a small developer would make a careful lender stop. In a company that size, the market kept lending for a while because size felt like safety.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the moment new credit stopped being available while the company still had very large numbers of homes sold and unfinished. From then on, each new sale was needed to pay for the last one, buyers became reluctant to buy from a developer that might not finish, and falling sales removed the cash that the unfinished buildings needed. A pre-sale model running in reverse is very hard to stop.

7. Root cause

Roman's view. The root cause was a structural mismatch, not a market accident. Buyers' money was short-term in character, because buyers expected a home within a few years, while the uses it was put to, land banks and unrelated businesses, were long-term and illiquid. The protection that should have stood between the two, money held for each building until that building was done, was weak or bypassed. A sketch with hypothetical round numbers shows the mechanism at small scale. A developer pre-sells a project and collects 10,000,000 dollars of deposits. If those deposits sit in trust or insured escrow, a market fall leaves the building fundable by its loan and the buyers protected. If instead 6,000,000 dollars is spent on a new site, the first project now has a 6,000,000-dollar hole that only new sales can fill. The second project has the same problem a year later, and the hole grows with every success.

What a small developer can see from this

You will never run a company of that size, and the lesson is easier to apply because of it. Ask three questions of your own business every quarter. Is any project's cash being used, even briefly, to cover another project's needs? Are any suppliers or contractors being asked to wait for payment so that your cash goes further? And is your plan for next year's equity dependent on this year's sales? A yes to any of them is the same mechanism in miniature. It feels like working capital management at the time. In a downturn, it is the reason one slow project takes the others with it.

The prevention rule

Rule 124: never let a buyer's deposit fund anything but the building it was paid for. Hold every deposit in trust, escrow or an arrangement your lawyer confirms is protected, sell only units the funded plan can finish, and never use pre-sale cash to buy land or start another project.

Cole's note on the legal side. Many jurisdictions regulate how pre-sale deposits are held, insured or released, and some allow limited use of deposits for construction with protections such as insurance. The rules differ and change; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it, and take local legal advice before you design a deposit arrangement.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating buyers' money as your liquidity. The control is ring-fencing: a separate trust or escrow account per project, a monthly reconciliation of deposits held against contracts signed, and a written rule that nothing leaves it except as the law and the contract allow.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads a large deposit balance as strength. A deposit balance is a measure of how many people you owe a finished home. Read it as an obligation.

Callback

In Week 46, I took you through leverage spirals and maturity walls. Evergrande adds a third ingredient: obligations to buyers that cannot be refinanced at all. A lender can be asked to extend. A family waiting for an apartment cannot be rolled over.

Recap

Evergrande used pre-sale cash to fund land and growth, credit tightened from 2020, it defaulted in late 2021 and was ordered wound up in early 2024, leaving many homes unfinished. The root cause was spending short-term, purpose-bound money on long-term uses. Rule 124 keeps every deposit with its own building.

Next: Priya on The Money: how pre-sales size the loan, the equity and the return.
checklist: Every project has its own deposit trust, escrow or protected account, confirmed by my lawyer.
Deposits held are reconciled against signed contracts every month.
No pre-sale cash is used to buy land or start another project.
I sell only units the funded plan can finish, including contingency.
Contractors and suppliers are paid in cash on contract terms, never in instruments or promises.
I watch my leverage and short-term debt as a share of equity every quarter.
I read my deposit balance as an obligation to deliver, not as liquidity.
head: Field checklist
speak: Evergrande did not fail because it could not sell homes. It sold homes before they were built and used the cash to buy land, start new projects and enter unrelated businesses, so every year had to be better than the last. When regulators tightened developer leverage in 2020 and credit dried up, the company struggled to pay suppliers, defaulted on offshore bonds in December 2021 and was ordered wound up by a Hong Kong court in January 2024, with many homes unfinished. The root cause was a mismatch: buyers' money was short-term and purpose-bound, and it was spent on long-term, illiquid uses. A deposit is not equity. It is an obligation to deliver a home. Rule 124: never let a buyer's deposit fund anything but the building it was paid for, hold every deposit in protected trust or escrow, and never use pre-sale cash for land or another project.
terms: Ring-fencing — keeping a project's money in separate accounts and legal arrangements so it cannot be used for other projects or reached by other creditors.
Deposit trust or escrow — an arrangement in which a buyer's deposit is held by a lawyer, trustee or escrow agent for the buyer until closing or another defined release event.
Liquidity mismatch — funding long-term, hard-to-sell uses with money that can be demanded back, or must be delivered against, in the short term.

hostile.q: As a potential equity partner, I see 10 million dollars of buyer deposits on your balance sheet. Why can you not use some of it to close the land deal we are discussing?
hostile.a: Because that money is not mine to invest. It is held in trust for buyers of a specific building and can leave the account only as the law and their contracts allow. Using it for land would create a hole in that building's funding that only future sales could fill. The new deal has to stand on its own equity and its own loan, and I would expect you to want the same discipline applied to your money.

rule: Rule 124: Never let a buyer's deposit fund anything but the building it was paid for; hold every deposit in a protected trust or escrow arrangement confirmed by counsel, sell only what the funded plan can finish, and never use pre-sale cash to buy land or start another project.

title: Pre-Sales Lock the Revenue and Leave the Cost Floating
summary: Pre-sales decide whether the construction loan funds at all, but they also fix the price of a large share of the building years before the cost is known. This lesson works through how a lender sizes pre-sales against the loan, what a cost rise does to a pre-sold project's margin and how buyer defaults enter the numbers.
body:
The moment you pre-sell a unit, its price is fixed and its cost is not. A pre-sold project is therefore a bet that your cost will hold, and the money question in every pre-sale campaign is how much of your margin you have locked in against a cost you have not yet locked down.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 124?

A. Never let a buyer's deposit fund anything but the building it was paid for; hold deposits in protected trust or escrow, sell only what the funded plan can finish, and never use pre-sale cash for land or another project.

Q. What is loan-to-cost?

A. The loan amount divided by the total project cost, a common way construction lenders limit how much they will lend.

Q. What is a guaranteed maximum price?

A. A contract price the contractor agrees not to exceed for the defined scope, with savings often shared and overruns borne by the contractor, subject to the contract's exclusions and change provisions.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in a for-sale project the lender does not lend against a building's income, because there will be none. It lends against the sale proceeds that will repay it. Pre-sales are its evidence that those proceeds exist. That makes the pre-sale campaign a financing event, and it means a pricing decision made in a sales office in month 3 can decide your return in month 30. You need to see both sides of that ledger at once.

How the lender sizes pre-sales

In plain English: the lender wants enough firm sales that, if the building is finished, the money from those buyers alone repays most or all of the loan.

The professional framing is pre-sale coverage: the net sale proceeds of qualifying contracts divided by the loan amount. Lenders set their own definition of a qualifying contract, for example a minimum deposit paid, no unusual conditions, an arm's-length buyer and limits on related-party or bulk buyers. The required coverage, and whether it is measured on units, revenue or net proceeds, is commercial practice negotiated deal by deal, not a standard.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. Total project cost is 40,000,000 dollars. The lender offers 70 percent loan-to-cost, a loan of 28,000,000 dollars. It requires qualifying pre-sales whose net proceeds equal 100 percent of the loan. Average price is 500,000 dollars a unit, and selling costs, commissions and closing costs, are 5 percent, so net proceeds are 475,000 dollars a unit. Units needed: 28,000,000 divided by 475,000, which is 58.9, so 59 qualifying sales. At a 10 percent deposit, those buyers will have paid about 2,950,000 dollars of deposits. Note what the deposits do not do. If they are held in trust, which is the norm in many places, they do not reduce your equity. You still fund the full 12,000,000 dollars of equity yourself, before the first loan draw.

Say that out loud now.

Reading the qualifying definition

The number of sales you need depends as much on what counts as on how many you sign. Lenders commonly exclude, or cap, several kinds of contract: sales to related parties, such as your relatives, partners or employees; bulk sales of several units to one buyer; sales with unusual conditions, such as a right to cancel if the buyer cannot sell another property; contracts where the deposit is not yet paid in full; and in some cases a share of sales to buyers abroad, because their financing is harder to confirm. Each exclusion is a commercial term, so negotiate it before the campaign starts, not in month 9.

A quick illustration. You sign 65 units, but 6 are to one investor company that exceeds the lender's bulk limit and 3 have deposits still outstanding. Qualifying sales are 56, below the 59 you need, and construction cannot start. Track qualifying sales as a separate line from signed sales from the first day.

The fixed-price squeeze

Here is the risk the sales team rarely sees. A second worked example on the same project. The building has 100 units at an average of 500,000 dollars, gross revenue 50,000,000 dollars. Less 5 percent selling costs, net revenue is 47,500,000 dollars. Against a cost of 40,000,000 dollars, profit is 7,500,000 dollars, a margin on cost of 18.75 percent.

Now construction costs rise, and total cost ends 8 percent higher, at 43,200,000 dollars. You have pre-sold 60 units at fixed prices, so only the 40 unsold units can be repriced. Profit at the original prices falls to 4,300,000 dollars, a margin of about 10 percent. To restore the original profit, the 40 unsold units would need to recover 3,200,000 dollars of net proceeds, which is 80,000 dollars each net, or about 84,000 dollars each in gross price, an increase of about 17 percent. Markets rarely give a developer that in a single phase. In practice, most of the cost rise comes out of your margin.

The control is to match the revenue you lock with the cost you lock. Before you pre-sell a large share of the building, fix as much of the construction cost as you can, with a guaranteed maximum price or fixed-price trade packages, and carry a contingency sized for what is still open. Some developers also cap the share of units sold before a fixed construction price is signed. That cap is a commercial choice, not a rule, and it trades speed for safety.

When buyers walk

Pre-sales transfer market risk only if buyers close. If prices fall between signing and completion, some buyers may refuse to close or fail to get a mortgage. What happens next is governed by the contract and local law; in many places the developer may keep some or all of the deposit and may also be able to claim further losses, but that varies and courts can intervene; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A quick illustration on the same numbers. Market prices fall 10 percent before completion, and 5 of the 60 pre-sold buyers default. Each forfeits a 50,000-dollar deposit, 250,000 dollars in all. You resell the 5 units at 450,000 dollars, receiving 2,137,500 dollars net after 5 percent selling costs, against 2,375,000 dollars you would have received net from the original buyers. The shortfall is 237,500 dollars, and the forfeited deposits cover it, just, with resale carry and delay still to pay. A smaller deposit, or a larger fall, and they would not. Deposit size is therefore a risk control, not only a sales term.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, pre-sales should change nothing until closing. The deposits are not your assets; they are held for buyers. The profit is not earned until units close and the loan is repaid. What does belong on your balance sheet is the risk: any cost-overrun or completion guarantee you signed to get the loan, and the equity you have committed. A useful habit is to show a for-sale project at the equity you put in, with a note of the guarantees beside it, and to record profit only when it is received. A licensed adviser is required before you act on how to report or plan around it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pre-selling most of a building on fixed prices before its cost is fixed. The control is a written rule linking the share of units sold to the share of construction cost under fixed price, reviewed at every release.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats deposits as equity and plans to use them. In many places they cannot be used, and where they can, the protections are strict. Plan your equity as if every deposit stays in trust until closing.

Callback

In Week 51, Quincy taught escalation in cost plans. Today shows its sharpest edge. Escalation in a rental project lowers yield on cost but can be offset by higher rents later. Escalation in a pre-sold project falls almost entirely on your margin, because the revenue was fixed before the cost moved.

Recap

Lenders size pre-sales as net proceeds covering a share of the loan; here, 59 sales covered a 28,000,000-dollar loan. Pre-sales fix revenue while cost floats, so an 8 percent cost rise cut margin from 18.75 to about 10 percent. Lock cost before you lock revenue, and size deposits to cover defaults.

Next: LEX on The Rules: disclosure, deposits and consumer protection in pre-sales.
checklist: I know the lender's definition of a qualifying pre-sale and the coverage it requires.
I have calculated how many qualifying sales repay the loan at net proceeds.
My equity plan assumes every deposit stays in trust until closing.
I link the share of units sold to the share of construction cost under fixed price.
I have stress-tested margin for a cost rise with only unsold units repriceable.
Deposit size is set to cover a realistic default and resale loss.
Pre-sold profit appears on my balance sheet only when units close.
head: Field checklist
speak: A pre-sold unit has a fixed price and a floating cost. Lenders size pre-sales by coverage: the net proceeds of qualifying contracts divided by the loan. In my hypothetical, a 28 million dollar loan at 475,000 dollars of net proceeds per unit needed 59 qualifying sales. Those buyers' deposits, held in trust, do not reduce my equity. The squeeze comes when cost rises. With 60 of 100 units sold at fixed prices, an 8 percent cost rise cut my margin from 18.75 percent to about 10, and the unsold units would need a 17 percent price rise to recover it. So I lock cost before I lock revenue, with a guaranteed maximum price or fixed-price packages, and I cap the share of units sold until cost is fixed. Deposits are also a risk control: they have to be large enough to cover a buyer walking away in a falling market.
terms: Pre-sale coverage — the net sale proceeds of qualifying pre-sale contracts divided by the loan amount.
Qualifying pre-sale — a sale contract that meets the lender's conditions, such as a minimum deposit paid, an arm's-length buyer and no unusual conditions.
Margin on cost — profit divided by total development cost, a common measure of return on a for-sale project.

hostile.q: You have pre-sold 60 percent at fixed prices but your construction contract is still a cost-plus estimate. What happens to my loan if costs rise 10 percent?
hostile.a: The loan stays repaid, because pre-sale coverage is above 100 percent of the loan on net proceeds, but my margin takes the hit. That is why I am not releasing more units until a guaranteed maximum price is signed, and why the budget carries a contingency sized for the open packages. If cost rises before then, I fund it as equity under my cost-overrun guarantee, and the in-balance test protects you.

title: The Rules Around Selling a Home That Does Not Exist Yet
summary: Selling off plan is one of the most regulated things a developer does, because the buyer pays for something they cannot inspect. This lesson sets out the main families of rule as concepts: disclosure and cooling-off, deposit protection, honest marketing, buyer verification, and the point at which a home sale becomes an investment offering.
body:
The law treats an off-plan buyer as someone paying real money for a promise they cannot inspect, so nearly every rule in pre-sales exists to make the promise clear, keep the money safe and stop the seller from overstating what is being sold.

Recall

Q. What is pre-sale coverage?

A. The net sale proceeds of qualifying pre-sale contracts divided by the loan amount; lenders set the required coverage as a commercial term.

Q. What is misrepresentation in contract law?

A. A false statement of fact that induces someone to enter a contract. Depending on whether it was innocent, careless or deliberate, it can allow the contract to be undone and damages to be claimed.

Q. From Week 70, what makes something a security?

A. Broadly, an investment of money in a common enterprise with an expectation of profit from the efforts of others; the exact tests differ by jurisdiction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the pre-sale contract is the most important document you will sign with the public. It can be signed by hundreds of people, it lasts for years and every word in your marketing can be read back into it by a court. A developer who gets the rules wrong does not usually face one claim. He faces the same claim from every buyer at once. This lesson teaches concepts and how to think, not what any jurisdiction requires. Verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it, and have a real estate lawyer admitted where you sell draft the contract and review the marketing.

Family one: disclosure and cooling-off

In plain English: before the buyer is bound, you must tell them the important facts in writing, and in many places they get a few days to change their mind.

The professional framing is the disclosure statement: a document, required by statute in many places for new condominium or strata projects, describing the developer, the project, the budget for common expenses, the planned completion date, the deposit arrangements, any material encumbrances and the buyer's rights. Many regimes add a cooling-off or rescission period, during which the buyer can cancel and recover the deposit, sometimes starting only once the disclosure has been delivered [unverified — confirm independently]. Some require an amended disclosure when a material fact changes, which may restart the buyer's right to cancel.

A worked example, hypothetical. You sign 30 buyers in the first month. In month 4 the planned amenity floor is redesigned to add 6 units, and the projected common expense budget rises 15 percent. Under many disclosure regimes that is a material change. If you do not issue an amended disclosure, buyers may later argue they can cancel because they were never told. If you do issue it, some may have a fresh right to cancel. The right answer is almost always to disclose promptly and price that risk, because the alternative is a defect in every contract you have signed.

Family two: deposit protection

Deposits are usually the most heavily regulated money in the project. Common patterns include a requirement that deposits be held in trust by a lawyer or licensed agent, limits on how and when they can be released, interest rules, and in some places a deposit insurance or new-home warranty programme that protects buyers if the developer fails [unverified — confirm independently]. Some regimes allow deposits to be used for construction if they are insured or bonded. The details differ widely; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Your discipline is the same everywhere: a written deposit arrangement agreed before the first sale, a trust or escrow holder independent of you, a reconciliation of deposits held to contracts signed, and no release except as the law and the contract allow. Rule 124 is the commercial version of this family of law.

Say that out loud now.

Family three: honest marketing

Every brochure, rendering, floor plan, view simulation and sentence a salesperson says can become evidence. Many places have consumer protection laws against misleading advertising that apply alongside the general law of misrepresentation. The safe framing is that marketing must be literally true, not misleading by what it leaves out, and consistent with the contract.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Your brochure shows an unobstructed ocean view from the upper floors. A site next door is zoned for a taller building, which you know. Even if the contract says renderings are illustrative, a court may treat a known, material omission as misleading. The control is a marketing review: every image and claim checked by the design team for accuracy and by your lawyer for risk, with disclaimers that are prominent, specific and true, not a sentence in small print that contradicts the picture above it.

Family four: buyer verification

Anti-money-laundering rules in many places require real estate professionals, and sometimes developers, to verify the identity of buyers and the source of funds, keep records and report suspicious transactions. Some places also restrict or tax purchases by non-residents. A buyer abroad, including a diaspora buyer, is not suspicious for being abroad, but verification takes longer, and funds arriving from an unrelated third party or in unusual patterns must be questioned. Verify the rules that apply to you against the primary source before you rely on them.

Family five: assignment, resale and price changes

Off-plan contracts often deal with three more questions, and each is a source of disputes. Assignment: may a buyer sell their contract to someone else before completion? Many developers restrict it, require consent or charge a fee, and some places tax or regulate assignment profits [unverified — confirm independently]. Changes: what may the developer change after signing, such as finishes, floor area or the completion date, and what happens if the change exceeds a stated tolerance? Many contracts allow small changes and give the buyer a remedy for large ones. Delay: what happens if completion runs late? Some regimes set outside dates after which a buyer may cancel and recover the deposit. Write all three questions into the contract deliberately, because a vague clause invites every buyer to read it in their own favour.

A short illustration, hypothetical. The contract allows the final floor area to differ by up to 2 percent without a price adjustment. A redesign reduces a unit by 3 percent. That unit is outside the tolerance, and the buyer's remedy, a price reduction, a right to cancel or both, depends on the clause. If 20 units are affected, the redesign has created 20 negotiations. Price the tolerance before you redesign.

The line between a home and a security

The most dangerous drafting mistake in pre-sales is turning a home sale into an investment offering. If a unit is marketed with a guaranteed rental return, a mandatory rental pool run by you, or profit-sharing from hotel operations, the arrangement may meet the tests for a security in many places, which can bring registration, prospectus or exemption requirements and serious liability [unverified — confirm independently]. Week 70 covered the concepts. The practical rule is simple: if the pitch is about the return rather than the home, stop and take securities advice before anything is printed or said.

Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer admitted where you sell, for the contract and disclosure; a securities lawyer before any rental pool, return guarantee or investment-style marketing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a defect copied into every contract: a missing disclosure, an unprotected deposit or a misleading promise repeated to every buyer. The control is a pre-launch legal review of the contract, the disclosure, the deposit arrangement and every piece of marketing, signed off before the first sale and repeated whenever any of them changes.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes the disclaimer protects him. A disclaimer cannot make a misleading picture true. Make the picture true.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught what binds in a contract and what does not. Pre-sales test that at scale. A reservation form, a deposit receipt and a signed purchase agreement may carry very different legal force, and your sales team must know which one a buyer has signed.

Recap

Four families of rule govern pre-sales: disclosure and cooling-off, deposit protection, honest marketing and buyer verification, with a fifth line where a home sale with promised returns becomes a security. Each varies by place, so review the contract, disclosure, deposits and marketing with local counsel before the first sale.

Next: Sage on The Numbers: reverse engineering the price a pre-sale campaign must achieve.
checklist: A real estate lawyer admitted where I sell has drafted the contract and disclosure.
I know whether a cooling-off or rescission period applies and when it starts.
Every material change triggers a review of whether an amended disclosure is required.
The deposit trust or escrow arrangement is in writing before the first sale.
Every rendering, floor plan and marketing claim has been checked for accuracy and by counsel.
Buyer identity and source of funds are verified and recorded under the applicable rules.
No rental guarantee, rental pool or return-based marketing is used without securities advice.
My sales team knows the legal difference between a reservation, a deposit receipt and a contract.
head: Field checklist
speak: The law treats an off-plan buyer as someone paying for a promise they cannot inspect, so pre-sale rules make the promise clear, keep the money safe and stop the seller overstating it. There are four families. Disclosure and cooling-off: many places require a written disclosure statement and give the buyer days to cancel, and a material change may need an amended disclosure. Deposit protection: deposits are usually held in trust, with strict release rules and sometimes insurance or warranty programmes. Honest marketing: every image and claim must be literally true and not misleading by omission, and a disclaimer cannot fix a misleading picture. Buyer verification: identity and source of funds must be checked. And one line I never cross without securities advice: if the pitch is about a guaranteed return or a rental pool rather than the home, it may be a security. All of this varies by place, so local counsel reviews everything before the first sale.
terms: Disclosure statement — a document, often required by statute for new condominium projects, setting out the material facts about the project, the developer and the buyer's rights.
Cooling-off period — a set time after signing, or after receiving disclosure, during which a buyer may cancel and recover the deposit, where the law provides one.
Rental pool — an arrangement in which owners' units are rented out together and income is shared, which can raise securities law questions.

hostile.q: Your broker wants to advertise a guaranteed 7 percent rental yield for the first three years. That will sell units. Why not?
hostile.a: Because a guaranteed return turns the conversation from buying a home to making an investment, and in many places that can make the arrangement a security, with registration duties and personal liability if anything is misstated. It also creates a promise I would have to fund if rents fell short. I will not approve it unless a securities lawyer has reviewed it, and I would rather sell the home on what it actually is.

title: Reverse Engineering the Price a Pre-Sale Campaign Must Achieve
summary: Start from the finished outcome you need, a target margin and a loan that funds on time, and work backward to the average price, the price ladder, the selling pace and the deposit size that deliver it. This lesson works one hypothetical project step by step, with units.
body:
Most developers set prices by looking at the market and hoping the margin follows. Do it the other way round: start with the margin and the loan you need, work backward to the price and pace that deliver them, and only then ask whether the market will pay it.

Recall

Q. What is a disclosure statement in a pre-sale?

A. A document, required by statute for new condominium projects in many places, setting out the material facts about the project and the buyer's rights, often linked to a cooling-off period.

Q. What is the fixed-price squeeze?

A. When pre-sold units are locked at fixed prices while construction cost is still open, so a cost rise falls almost entirely on the developer's margin.

Q. What is a residual land value?

A. The most you can pay for land, found by taking the finished value, subtracting all other costs and the required profit, and treating what is left as the land budget.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even week, so we reverse engineer. You did the same thing with land in Week 31 and with a design budget in Week 108. Pre-sale pricing is the same discipline applied to revenue. If you know the margin you need and the lender's conditions, the price is not a guess. It is an answer, and the market study then tells you whether that answer is achievable. If it is not, you know before you launch, not after six months of slow sales. Every figure here is hypothetical and round.

Step one: from target margin to required revenue

In plain English: decide the profit you need, add it to the cost, and gross it up for the cost of selling.

The project's total cost is 40,000,000 dollars. You require a margin on cost of 20 percent, which is 8,000,000 dollars of profit. Net revenue must therefore be 48,000,000 dollars. Selling costs, commissions, marketing and closing costs, are 5 percent of gross revenue, so gross revenue must be 48,000,000 divided by 0.95, which is about 50,526,000 dollars.

The building has 100 units totalling 8,000 square metres of saleable area. The required average price is 50,526,000 divided by 8,000, about 6,316 dollars per square metre, or about 505,260 dollars per 80-square-metre unit.

Now ask the market. If comparable new projects nearby are selling at 6,000 to 6,500 dollars per square metre, the target sits inside the range and the project can proceed. If they are selling at 5,500, the margin you need is not available at this cost, and you change the cost, the design or the land price before launch, not after.

Step two: from the average to the price ladder

You plan three tranches, as Remi taught on Day 1. The first is priced below the average to build momentum; the last must be priced above it to make the average work.

A worked example. Tranche 1: 30 units at 5 percent below the average, 480,000 dollars each, 14,400,000 dollars. Tranche 2: 30 units at the average, about 505,260 dollars each, about 15,158,000 dollars. Tranche 3: the remaining 40 units must bring in the rest: 50,526,000 minus 14,400,000 minus 15,158,000, which is about 20,968,000 dollars, or about 524,200 dollars each, 3.75 percent above the average.

That last number is the test. Will the market accept a 3.75 percent rise by the time tranche 3 is released, typically once construction is visibly under way? If your market study says prices are flat, the ladder does not work, and the opening discount is too deep.

Say that out loud now.

Step three: from the loan to the selling pace

The lender offers 28,000,000 dollars and requires qualifying pre-sales whose net proceeds cover 100 percent of the loan before first draw, a commercial term for this hypothetical. Net proceeds of tranches 1 and 2 are 14,400,000 plus 15,158,000, which is 29,558,000 dollars gross, times 0.95, about 28,080,000 dollars net. That just clears the requirement. So both tranches, 60 units, must be firmly sold before construction can start.

Now the pace. Your market study suggests absorption of about 5 units a month at the tranche 1 price and about 4 a month at the tranche 2 price. Tranche 1 takes 6 months; tranche 2 takes 7.5 months. Total, 13.5 months to reach the threshold.

Your budget assumed construction would start after 10 months of pre-sales and included 1,500,000 dollars of pre-construction carry, at 150,000 dollars a month. The extra 3.5 months cost 525,000 dollars, cutting profit to about 7,475,000 dollars and margin on cost to about 18.7 percent. Working backward again: to start in 10 months you need about 6 sales a month across the first 60 units. You either accept the lower margin, deepen the opening discount and test what it does to the ladder, negotiate a lower pre-sale threshold, or reduce carry. Each is now a priced choice.

Step four: from the default you can tolerate to the deposit

A second worked example. You want the forfeited deposit to cover your loss if a buyer walks away after a 10 percent fall in prices. A defaulting buyer's unit originally sold at about 505,000 dollars, about 480,000 dollars net. Resold at 10 percent less, about 455,000 dollars gross, it nets about 432,000 dollars. The shortfall is about 48,000 dollars, roughly 9.5 percent of the original price. Add a few months of carry and remarketing on the resold unit, say another 1 to 2 percent. The deposit you need is therefore at least about 11 percent of the price; a 10 percent deposit leaves a small gap, and a 15 percent deposit would cover a fall of about 14 percent. Deposits that size may slow sales, so this too is a priced trade, and how much of a deposit you can actually keep on default depends on the contract and local law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Step five: one line of sensitivity

Finish by asking which input moves the outcome most, because that is where you need the best evidence. On these numbers, a 1 percent change in the average price moves gross revenue by about 505,000 dollars and margin on cost by about 1.2 points. A 1 percent change in total cost moves margin by about 1.2 points as well. One extra month of pre-sales moves margin by about 0.4 points. A one-point change in selling costs moves margin by about 1.3 points. So price and cost dominate, and selling costs matter more than most developers expect, which is a reason to negotiate broker commissions and marketing budgets before launch with the same care you bring to the construction price. Write the four sensitivities on the price sheet, so that everyone who argues for a discount or a richer marketing budget can see what it costs in margin.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is launching at a price the market sets without checking it against the margin and the loan. The control is a one-page reverse-engineered price sheet, approved before launch: target margin, required average, ladder, pace to threshold, carry and deposit, each with the market evidence beside it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tests the average price and forgets the ladder. An average that only works if the last tranche sells well above the market is a hope, not a plan. Test the last tranche price on its own.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal from public information: implied land price, rent and return. Today you reverse engineered your own deal from the inside. The method is the same: fix the outcome, work back one equation at a time, and treat any step the market cannot support as the place to redesign.

Recap

From a 20 percent margin on 40,000,000 dollars of cost, gross revenue must be about 50,526,000 dollars, about 6,316 dollars per square metre. A three-tranche ladder needs the last tranche about 3.75 percent above average. The loan needs 60 sales; at the market's pace that is 13.5 months, costing about 1.3 points of margin. A deposit of about 11 percent covers a 10 percent fall.

Next: Remi in The Room: the launch meeting where the broker wants to promise too much.
checklist: I derive the required average price from target margin, cost and selling costs before launch.
I compare the required price per square metre with real comparable sales.
I test the last tranche price on its own, not only the average.
I calculate how many sales the lender's threshold requires and how long they take at realistic absorption.
I price the carry of a slower campaign against the cost of a deeper discount.
Deposit size is set from the price fall I want it to cover, confirmed against local law.
The reverse-engineered price sheet is approved before the first unit is released.
head: Field checklist
speak: I reverse engineer pre-sale pricing from the outcome I need. In my hypothetical, cost is 40 million dollars and I need a 20 percent margin on cost, so net revenue must be 48 million and gross revenue about 50.5 million after 5 percent selling costs. Across 8,000 square metres, that is about 6,316 dollars per square metre, which I then test against comparable sales. With a three-tranche ladder, opening at 5 percent below average, the last 40 units must sell about 3.75 percent above average, and I test that price on its own. The lender needs net proceeds covering the 28 million dollar loan, which means 60 firm sales. At the market's pace that takes 13.5 months instead of 10, costing 525,000 dollars and about 1.3 points of margin. Finally, to cover a buyer walking away after a 10 percent price fall, the deposit needs to be about 11 percent.
terms: Required average price — the average sale price, usually per square metre, that delivers the target margin after cost and selling costs.
Tranche — a group of units released for sale together at a set price, as one step of a price ladder.
Selling costs — commissions, marketing and closing costs, often modelled as a percentage of gross revenue.

hostile.q: Your last tranche has to sell 3.75 percent above your average. What happens if the market goes flat?
hostile.a: Then margin falls, and I have measured by how much. If tranche 3 sells at the average instead, revenue falls by about 760,000 dollars and margin on cost falls from 20 percent to about 18. That still repays the loan, because the first 60 sales cover it on net proceeds. If the market weakens further before tranche 3, I hold those units back, finish the building and sell completed units, which usually price better than off-plan, rather than discount into a falling market.

title: The Launch Meeting Where the Broker Wants to Promise Too Much
summary: Before a pre-sale campaign starts, you meet the sales broker, the marketing lead and your lawyer to approve the launch. The broker arrives with four ideas that would sell units faster and each would break a rule. This lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say and the question behind each request, and closes with a monthly note on ethics.
body:
The launch meeting decides what will be said to hundreds of buyers in your name. Approve only what is true, protected and written down, and say no early, plainly and without heat, because every yes in this room is repeated in every sales conversation that follows.

Recall

Q. In yesterday's reverse engineering, how many sales did the lender's threshold require, and why?

A. Sixty, because the net proceeds of the first two tranches, about 28,080,000 dollars, were the first point at which qualifying sales covered the 28,000,000-dollar loan.

Q. What is the line between a home sale and a security in pre-sales?

A. If the pitch is about a return, such as a guaranteed rental yield or a mandatory rental pool, rather than about the home, it may meet the tests for a security, which needs securities advice before anything is said or printed.

Q. What is acknowledge, bridge, answer?

A. A way to handle a hard question: acknowledge the concern, bridge to the relevant fact or principle, then answer directly.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this scene teaches how to run an internal meeting. It does not script anything to say to a real buyer or investor, and it should not be used that way. In the room: the external sales broker who will run the campaign on commission, the marketing agency lead, your real estate lawyer and your finance lead. You chair. The disclosure, contract and deposit arrangement are drafted. The broker wants to launch in two weeks and has four ideas to speed it up.

Hold your state before you start. A broker's ideas are not hostile; they come from a commission paid on signatures, which is exactly the incentive you studied in Week 3. Your job is to keep that incentive pointed at sales that close.

Request one: the guaranteed yield

The broker: "Buyers abroad want income. If we guarantee a 7 percent rental yield for three years, we can sell the first tranche in a month."

The question behind the question: will the owner fund sales speed with a promise he may have to pay?

Say: "I understand why it would sell. We will not offer a guaranteed return. It would change what we are selling from a home to an investment, which raises securities questions, and it is a liability I would carry if rents fell short." Turn to your lawyer: "Is there anything about rental potential we can say accurately?" Let the lawyer answer.

Never say: "Let us call it an estimate instead of a guarantee." A number presented to sell an investment is still a number about an investment.

Request two: the convenient account

The broker: "Overseas buyers find wire transfers awkward. Let them pay deposits to our agency account abroad and we will forward them."

The question behind the question: will deposits pass through hands that are not the trust holder?

Say: "Every deposit goes directly to the trust holder named in the contract, from an account in the buyer's own name, with identity and source of funds verified. Nothing passes through the agency." Rule 124 and the deposit law both sit behind that sentence.

Say that out loud now.

Request three: the quiet discount

The broker: "For the first ten buyers, let me offer a further 3 percent off by side letter. It will not appear in the price list."

The question behind the question: will the sales ledger stop being the truth?

Say: "Any incentive is fine if it is in the price list, the contract and the sales ledger, and reported to the lender. A side letter that the lender does not see makes our reported prices untrue, and a qualifying sale may no longer qualify." Turn to your finance lead: "What does a 3 percent discount on ten units do to the ladder?" On the hypothetical numbers from Day 5, about 144,000 dollars, which tranche 3 must recover. Let the number sit.

Stay silent after that number. The room will usually reach the right decision itself.

Request four: the start date

The marketing lead: "The brochure should say construction starts next quarter. It gives buyers confidence."

The question behind the question: will we state as fact something that depends on conditions not yet met?

Say: "Construction starts when the loan's conditions are satisfied, including the pre-sale threshold. We can describe the plan and its conditions accurately. We will not state a date as a fact." Ask the lawyer whether the disclosure already describes the conditions; it should, and the brochure must agree with it.

Never say: "Everyone in the market says that." What others say does not change what your contract and your disclosure must say.

When the broker pushes back

The broker leans back: "With respect, you will be the only project in the market without these offers. Buyers will walk across the street." This is the moment the room tests whether your no was a position or a principle.

Acknowledge, bridge, answer. Say: "That may be true for some buyers, and we will lose a few. The buyers we keep will close, and the sales we report to the lender will be the sales we have. If the pace is too slow at our prices, we will change the price openly, not the terms quietly." Then ask a question that moves the conversation forward: "What would you need from us, within those limits, to hit five sales a month?" A broker who has been heard usually becomes useful again. A broker who has been overruled without a reason usually finds a way around you.

Closing the meeting

Read back the decisions: no guaranteed returns, deposits direct to the trust holder only, every incentive recorded and reported, no unconditional start date. Ask the lawyer to review the final brochure and the broker's sales script before launch, and ask the broker to share its buyer identity process. Agree how the broker will be paid: a structure that pays part of the commission at signing and the rest at closing aligns the broker with sales that complete. That is a commercial choice; agree it in writing.

Ethics and anti-corruption, a monthly thread

Pre-sales put small temptations in front of good people every week: a broker who offers a personal referral fee for steering a contract to them, a buyer who wants a backdated price, an official who hints that approvals would move faster with a favour. Each one is small, and each one turns a business that depends on public trust into one that depends on secrecy. The anti-bribery and integrity concepts from Week 72 apply here exactly, and many jurisdictions treat facilitation of a bribe, not only payment of one, as an offence; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A practical habit is to decide your answers before the offer arrives and to write them into a short code for everyone who sells in your name: no undisclosed payments, no side letters, no gifts above a stated small value, and every unusual request reported to you the same day. The cost of saying no is a slower sale. The cost of saying yes is a reputation you cannot buy back.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is approving a sales practice because it is common in the market. The control is a launch checklist signed by your lawyer, covering the contract, the disclosure, the deposit route, every marketing piece and the broker's script, reviewed again at every new tranche.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leaves the broker to run the campaign and reviews only the sales numbers. Every word the broker says is said for you. Review the words.

Callback

In Week 3, Kema taught that incentives explain most behaviour in a deal. The broker in this room is not dishonest; he is paid on signatures. Each of his four ideas follows from that incentive, and each of your answers points the incentive back toward contracts that close lawfully.

Recap

Four requests, one principle. No guaranteed returns, deposits only to the trust holder, every incentive recorded, no unconditional start date. Pay the broker in a way that rewards closings, and write an integrity code before the first temptation arrives.

Next: Kema on the week in review, with Cole in the Auditor's Chair.
checklist: I have stated in writing that no guaranteed return or rental pool will be offered without securities advice.
Every deposit goes directly to the named trust holder from an account in the buyer's own name.
Every incentive appears in the price list, the contract and the sales ledger, and is reported to the lender.
No marketing states a construction start date as fact before the loan conditions are met.
My lawyer reviews the brochure and the broker's script before launch and at each new tranche.
The broker's commission is split between signing and closing, in writing.
Everyone who sells in my name has a short written integrity code.
head: Field checklist
speak: The launch meeting decides what will be said to hundreds of buyers in my name. The broker, paid on signatures, brings four ideas. A guaranteed rental yield: no, because it turns a home into an investment and creates a liability I would have to fund. Deposits through the agency's account abroad: no, every deposit goes directly to the trust holder from the buyer's own account, with identity verified. A quiet discount by side letter: no, because any incentive must be in the price list, the contract and the ledger, and reported to the lender, or our reported prices stop being true. A firm construction start date in the brochure: no, construction starts when the loan conditions are met, and we describe those conditions accurately. I close by having my lawyer review the brochure and the script, and I split the broker's commission between signing and closing so that the incentive rewards sales that actually complete.
terms: Side letter — a separate agreement that changes the terms of a main contract, which becomes a problem when it is hidden from a lender or regulator.
Commission split — paying an agent part of the fee at contract signing and the rest at closing, to align the agent with completed sales.
Integrity code — a short written set of rules for everyone who acts in your name, covering payments, gifts, side deals and reporting of unusual requests.

hostile.q: As your broker, I am telling you competitors offer guaranteed yields and quiet discounts. You will lose buyers. Why tie my hands?
hostile.a: Because I would rather sell slightly slower and close every sale than sell faster and defend every contract. A guaranteed yield is a liability and possibly a securities issue, and a hidden discount makes the numbers I report to my lender untrue. You can offer any incentive that is recorded and reported, and I will pay part of your commission at closing so we are both rewarded for the same thing.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 124 Review: Pre-Sales, With Cole in the Auditor's Chair
summary: This review tests the week on pre-sales: what they do, how they size the loan, why deposits stay with their building, the rules that govern off-plan selling and how to reverse engineer a price. Cole then reads a hypothetical monthly sales report as a hostile auditor would, and the boardroom drill asks you to explain pre-sales in two minutes.
body:
Pre-sales come down to one discipline: sell only what is true, keep the money with the building it was paid for, and count closings rather than signatures. Today you test that, then watch an auditor take a sales report apart.

Recall

Q. In the launch meeting, why did you split the broker's commission between signing and closing?

A. Because a commission paid only at signing rewards contracts that may never close; paying part at closing aligns the broker with sales that complete lawfully.

Q. What is a hold point?

A. A step in the inspection and test plan at which work must stop until a named inspector has inspected and signed it off.

Q. From Week 41, what is buyer default in a pre-sale?

A. A buyer's failure to close or to pay as the contract requires, after which the developer's remedies, such as keeping the deposit or claiming further loss, depend on the contract and local law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Kema. The pre-sale campaign is the first time your project meets the public, and the first time your reporting is read by people with an interest in finding fault: the lender's credit officer, a buyers' lawyer if anything goes wrong, and an auditor. This review rehearses the explanations you will need and shows you how a hostile reader looks at your own sales report.

The six questions

Question 1. What three jobs does a pre-sale do, and when does it fail to do them?

Answer: It proves demand to a lender, discovers the price and transfers some market risk to buyers. It fails when deposits are too small, contracts do not bind or buyers are not real, because then nobody closes when the market turns.

Question 2. How does a lender size pre-sales?

Answer: By coverage: the net proceeds of qualifying contracts divided by the loan. In the hypothetical, a 28,000,000-dollar loan at 475,000 dollars net per unit needed 59 qualifying sales. The required coverage is a commercial term, negotiated deal by deal.

Question 3. Why is pre-selling dangerous to margin?

Answer: Because revenue is fixed while cost floats. With 60 of 100 units sold, an 8 percent cost rise cut margin on cost from 18.75 to about 10 percent. So I lock construction cost before I lock most of the revenue.

Question 4. What is Rule 124?

Answer: Never let a buyer's deposit fund anything but the building it was paid for; hold every deposit in protected trust or escrow, sell only what the funded plan can finish, and never use pre-sale cash for land or another project. It comes from Evergrande.

Question 5. Name the four families of pre-sale rules and the fifth line.

Answer: Disclosure and cooling-off, deposit protection, honest marketing and buyer verification. The fifth line is that a home sold with a guaranteed return or rental pool may become a security. Each varies by place and needs local counsel.

Question 6. How do you set the deposit size?

Answer: From the price fall I want it to cover. A 10 percent fall left a shortfall of about 9.5 percent of price plus carry, so about 11 percent covers it, subject to how much the contract and local law let me keep.

Say that out loud now.

Recap

Remi framed a pre-sale as a promise sold before the product exists, priced against absorption, released in tranches and sold through channels measured by cost per closed sale. Ford took Evergrande through seven steps: pre-sale cash funded land and growth, credit tightened and unfinished homes were left without money. Priya showed how pre-sales size the loan and squeeze margin. LEX set out the rules. Sage reverse engineered a price. Remi ran a launch meeting and said no four times.

Cole in the Auditor's Chair

Cole reads the hypothetical monthly sales report below as a hostile auditor would. Read it first and find the problems yourself.

Sales report, month 5. Units signed: 62 of 100. Pre-sale coverage: 112 percent of loan, calculated on gross contract prices. Deposits received: 3,100,000 dollars, of which 2,600,000 dollars held by the trust holder and 500,000 dollars in transit via the overseas agency. Incentives: standard price list applied. Note: 8 contracts signed by a single investor company; 4 buyers awaiting identity documents. Construction start: confirmed for next quarter.

Cole's findings. One: coverage is calculated on gross prices, not net proceeds after selling costs, which overstates it. On net proceeds the figure is lower, and the lender's definition decides which applies. Two: 500,000 dollars of deposits are held by the agency, not the trust holder, which breaks the deposit arrangement and probably the law; that money must be traced and moved today. Three: 8 contracts to one buyer may not qualify; many lenders cap bulk or related buyers, so the qualifying count may be 54, not 62. Four: 4 buyers have no verified identity, so those contracts should not be counted, and depending on the rules they should not have been accepted yet. Five: "standard price list applied" is a statement an auditor will test against the contracts; any side letter would make it false. Six: "construction start confirmed" is not true until loan conditions are met. The honest report is shorter and less flattering, and it is the only one a lender can rely on.

The boardroom drill

Explain pre-sales to a board in two minutes. Set a timer and speak before you read the model.

Model answer: "Pre-sales do three jobs. They prove demand to our lender, which requires firm sales covering the loan on net proceeds before first draw; they discover the price; and they transfer some market risk to buyers. They only work if deposits are meaningful, contracts are enforceable and buyers are verified, so we count closings, not signatures. Our price is reverse engineered from our margin and the loan, and the last tranche is tested on its own. Pre-sales fix revenue while cost floats, so we fix construction cost before we sell most of the building. Every deposit stays in trust with its own building, which is Rule 124, from Evergrande. And everything we say to buyers is reviewed by counsel, with no guaranteed returns and no side deals."

What a weak answer sounds like

Compare the model with a common weak version: "We are 62 percent sold, the market is strong, deposits are coming in well and we expect to start construction next quarter." Every clause invites a hard question. Sold on what definition? Strong against what comparable sales? Coming in where, and held by whom? Expect on what conditions? The weak answer is not dishonest; it is unanchored. Each sentence states a feeling where the board needs a fact with a source.

When you record yourself, listen for the words strong, well, about to and confident. Each one is usually standing where a number, a definition or a condition should be. Replace it, and record again. A board does not need you to be optimistic. It needs to know that your optimism has been checked by someone who was paid to doubt it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a flattering report: signatures counted as sales, gross counted as net and deposits counted wherever they happen to be. The control is to report to the lender's definitions, with exclusions shown.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner writes the sales report to reassure. Write it so that an auditor finds nothing you did not already say.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught that records made at the time are the evidence that wins. A pre-sale campaign creates hundreds of records in months: contracts, deposit receipts, identity checks and marketing approvals. Keep them as if every one will be read in a dispute, because some of them will be.

Recap

Pre-sales prove demand, discover price and transfer some risk, only if buyers close. Lock cost before revenue, keep deposits with their building, follow local rules on disclosure, deposits, marketing and verification, and report to the lender's definitions.

head: The six questions
speak: Pre-sales do three jobs: they prove demand to a lender, discover the price and transfer some market risk to buyers, but only if deposits are meaningful, contracts bind and buyers are verified. So I count closings, not signatures. Lenders size pre-sales by coverage on net proceeds; in my hypothetical, 59 sales covered a 28 million dollar loan. Pre-sales fix revenue while cost floats, so I fix construction cost before I sell most of the building. Rule 124, from Evergrande: a buyer's deposit funds only the building it was paid for, held in protected trust or escrow. The rules on disclosure, cooling-off, deposits, marketing and buyer verification vary by place, so counsel reviews everything, and I never offer a guaranteed return without securities advice. When Cole audits my sales report, he checks gross against net, where every deposit sits, bulk buyers, unverified buyers and every statement of fact.
terms: Bulk buyer — one buyer or group purchasing several units, often limited or excluded by lenders when counting qualifying pre-sales.
Net proceeds — the sale price less selling costs, commissions and closing costs, the figure most lenders use for coverage.
Auditor's Chair — reading your own document as a hostile auditor would, to find what is overstated, unsupported or untrue before someone else does.

hostile.q: As the lender's credit officer, your report says 62 sales and 112 percent coverage. My analyst says 54 qualifying sales and under 100 percent. Who is right?
hostile.a: Your analyst, on your definitions, and I should have reported it that way. Coverage should be on net proceeds, the single investor company's 8 contracts exceed your bulk-buyer limit, and 4 buyers are awaiting identity verification. I will reissue the report on your basis today, show every exclusion, and confirm that all deposits are now with the trust holder. We will not ask for first draw until qualifying coverage clears 100 percent.
